newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuanian markets calm on c.bank currency plans.
newsitem.headline: Lithuanian markets calm on c.bank currency plans.

text.p: Lithuanian financial analysts and dealers on Friday took new central bank plans for the litas currency calmly and saw no reason for currency instability.
The central bank unveiled long-awaited plans on Thursday to end the currency board system of regulating the litas but it said it would keep the litas fixed at four to one dollar.

"Lithuanian financial experts see no reason to devalue the litas and the stability of the currency is proved by the fall in average interest rates," Margarita Starkeviciute, a financial analyst who works for the central depository, told Reuters.
Dealers said the central bank's move influenced neither shares nor currency markets on Friday
Starkeviciute said that the stability of the currency was demonstrated by falling interest rates, rising GDP and a rising stock exchange index.
She said the bank's plans had been expected but that there were some doubts whether the bank's management had enough expertise to manage the switch to a new system.
The litas is currently pegged under a currency board, which commits the central bank to keep enough hard currency reserves in its vaults to back the local currency.
But the central bank is deprived of any powers to operate a monetary policy. The new plans are designed to give the bank back its powers and operate a peg without the currency board.
When new Prime Minister Gediminas Vagnorius came to power in November last year, he caused panic by saying he wanted to end the currency board at the start of this year.
But he later backtracked and the new plans have a more gradual phasing out of the currency board, which is enshrined in legislation that guarantees the peg.
"At present, it makes no difference what guarantees the stability of the litas -- the law or the Bank of Lithuania," said Arvydas Jacikevicius, a deal with leading broker Suprema.
"It is very good the position of the Bank of Lithuania was made clear since clarity always leads to stability," he said.
He said such moves before last year's elections may have caused instability but now the situation was calm.

"We expected such a decision by the Bank of Lithuania as it is in line with the programme of the new government and the new monetary policy did not influence the currency market as the litas remains at a fix of four to one dollar," Hermis Bank currency department deputy director Jonas Irzikevicius said.
